PS-320-task.text:
Dominant task (SCAN-14): judge his engineering from the decisions, then decide to interview or contact (hiring manager, tech lead; desktop). Recruiter scans title, tools, tenure; designer peer browses on a phone.
Option PS, round 10. Copy priority, top down: who he is (a general line from his CV, not one project), years, title; then who he has worked with; then About, where a decision comes before the platform name (journey: About and each Main Project). Figures such as the 40,000-enrolment load test stay inside their project. Phone history stays the moving strip.
Answered: Q1 one page, 5 sections · Q2 LinkedIn dates, CV roles · Q3 fold 765 / 568 · Q4 44×44 · Q5 iZone, Digital Form, MyInsights · Q6 timeline, then Minor. Round 10 feedback: the hero says who he is, not one project; the load-test figure belongs in the project; check copy priority.

PS-320-fail.text:
Self-check · still failing
• SCAN-01 / PRIO-02: the first Main Project decision starts at 2284 px (fold 568).
• Proposal: "the site describes his decisions first, such as row locking under enrolment load, and names the platform second." The hero now names OutSystems (the title) before any decision (your call). The About text must carry that decision (journey: About and each Main Project).
• Journey, Recruiter stage 1 "Title and tools, right there": title on screen one; first Tools line at 2388 px.
• HIER-03: two strips move on this page (Worked with and History), and motion pulls the eye. They drift in opposite directions, slowly, each with Pause.
• Spec "Follow his career" / Rule 7: the phone history drops each period's tools and months to stay minimal; tools still show on every project.
• Proposal, Decisions on record: "a displayed mark can imply the client endorses him". Marks that loop past keep that risk (his call).
• GRID-03: the bento mixes tile sizes on purpose, so density is uneven; CPLX-01: 13 tiles in one section.
• Proposal: "Marks are the only images." Poster art breaks this unless drawn in code; Rule 10 bars "an image of his work" (your call).
• Details: "describes him in his own voice". The first-person lines are drafts reworded from his facts, not his words; he approves or rewrites each.
